title: Reservations in two countries
summary: MesaLista books tables at 2,000 restaurants in Mexico and Texas. Payments need transactions and favorites are written in both countries.

requirements.1: {{s1}} keeps payments in managed MySQL without leaving Mexico, with a copy in another zone that takes over on its own if the primary fails.
requirements.2: {{s2}} gives reporting a separate copy of the slot 1 primary so it does not slow it down, even if the copy runs a few seconds behind.
requirements.3: {{s3}} stores favorites: each country writes in milliseconds to its own region and both accept writes. The other region sees them later, because availability is preferred over consistency.
requirements.4: {{s4}} alerts the reporting team if the slot 2 copy falls more than 30 seconds behind the primary.
requirements.5: {{s5}} keeps the database password out of the code: the app requests it at startup and the service sends a notice every 30 days that it is time to change it, so your own code changes it.
requirements.6: The pilot restaurant's MySQL runs on its own premises; its payments are migrated to slot 1 before opening to all 2,000 restaurants.

s1.explanation: Cloud SQL with HA has a primary and a secondary zone in the region; synchronous replication copies every write to the disks in both zones and, if the primary fails, Cloud SQL switches to the standby on its own.

s2.explanation: A Cloud SQL read replica is read-only, is updated in almost real time and serves queries and analytics, which lowers the load on the primary.

s3.explanation: Bigtable is available in northamerica-south1 and us-south1, replicates across clusters in up to 8 regions and allows reads and writes in each one; with multi-cluster routing it goes to the nearest cluster, and by default replication is eventually consistent.

s4.explanation: Cloud SQL measures the lag with the replica_lag metric, in seconds; a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy with a threshold condition on that metric notifies the team when it goes over 30 seconds.

s5.explanation: Secret Manager stores the password as a secret; with a rotation period it sends the SECRET_ROTATE message to Pub/Sub, and your subscriber is the one that changes it. Secret Manager does not rotate it by itself.

gcp-cloud-sql-ha.s2: The HA standby cannot be used for read queries; it only waits to take the primary's place.

gcp-cloud-sql-replica.s1: A read replica does not provide failover: it is read-only and you have to promote it to make it a primary.

gcp-spanner.s1: Spanner is not managed MySQL: it is a different database, with external consistency.
gcp-spanner.s2: Spanner is a different database; it is not a copy of the slot 1 MySQL.
gcp-spanner.s3: Spanner provides external consistency, stricter than strong consistency: it puts consistency first, and here the other region may see favorites later.

gcp-audit-logs.s4: Cloud Audit Logs records administrative activities and resource access (who did what, where and when); a threshold alert on the replica_lag metric is a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy.

gcp-parameter-manager.s5: Parameter Manager, an extension of Secret Manager, stores workload parameters and does not support rotation; the Pub/Sub rotation notices belong to Secret Manager.
